title: Inflation Explained: Why Your Money Quietly Shrinks
description:
Inflation explained simply: what the Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures, why US prices rose 3.7% in the year to September 2026, and why $10,000 in cash lost about $360 of buying power. We cover the 9.1% peak of June 2022, what causes inflation, why the Fed targets 2%, who wins and who loses, and what you can do: emergency savings, TIPS and I bonds, and long-term investing.

Assumptions: the $10,000 example uses the CPI-U index for September 2025 (324.800) and September 2026 (336.940). The 3.5% savings rate, the $2,000 fixed mortgage payment and the 3% inflation rate in the 20-year and mortgage examples are illustrations, not quotes or forecasts. Savings examples are before tax. The Fed's target range is as of 25 Nov 2026 (3.75%–4%; its next decision is 9 Dec 2026). The I bond rate of 5.51% applies to the first six months; the 1.40% fixed part lasts for the life of the bond. There is no 12-month CPI figure for October 2026 because October 2025 prices were not collected during the 2025 government shutdown.

scenes.say: Ten thousand dollars in a drawer quietly lost about three hundred and sixty dollars over the latest year of US price data. Nobody took a single bill.

visual.label: buying power lost by $10,000 in cash

scenes.say: On paper, it's still ten thousand. But at today's prices, it buys only what about nine thousand six hundred and forty bought a year ago.
That's inflation. It never sends you a bill. It just shrinks what every dollar can do.
Here's what you'll learn. What inflation really measures. What causes it. Who wins and who loses. And what you can actually do about it.

visual.title: What you'll learn
items: What you can do about it

scenes.say: And by the end, you'll see why some people actually come out ahead when prices rise, and how to tell which side you're on.
Chapter one. What inflation actually is.
Inflation is a rise in prices across the whole economy. Not one thing getting pricier, but most things, over time. So each dollar buys a little less.

visual.text:
Prices go up.
Each dollar buys less.

scenes.say: In the US, it's measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Every month, it records the prices of about eighty thousand items, sorted into more than two hundred categories.
Rent, groceries, gas, car insurance, doctor visits, phone bills. Together they form a basket, and the price of that basket is the Consumer Price Index, or C-P-I.

The basket is weighted by what households actually spend. Shelter, meaning rent and the rental value of owned homes, is the biggest piece, about thirty-six percent. Food is about fourteen. Energy, about six.

visual.title: What's in the US price basket (CPI-U)

scenes.say: The headline number compares the basket with a year earlier. In September twenty twenty-five, the index stood at three twenty-four point eight. By September twenty twenty-six, three thirty-six point nine. A rise of three point seven percent. Sounds small. So is it?
Chapter two. The real numbers.
Three point seven percent is the latest yearly figure, for September twenty twenty-six. That's well above the Federal Reserve's goal of two percent, which uses a slightly different measure.

visual.label: US inflation, 12 months to Sept 2026
visual.sub: CPI-U · Bureau of Labor Statistics, 14 Oct 2026

scenes.say: And if you're looking for October's number, there isn't one. The twenty twenty-five government shutdown meant October twenty twenty-five prices were never collected, so there's nothing to compare against. The next report is due December tenth.

visual.text:
"BLS did not collect survey data
for October 2025"
visual.source: BLS notice, 10 Nov 2026 · no 12-month figure for October 2026

scenes.say: Now zoom out. From twenty fifteen to twenty twenty, yearly inflation mostly stayed around two percent or less. Then it jumped. Four point seven percent in twenty twenty-one, and eight percent for twenty twenty-two as a whole.

visual.title: US inflation by year (annual average)
visual.note: Source: BLS CPI-U annual averages, via Minneapolis Fed

scenes.say: The worst moment came in June twenty twenty-two. Prices were up nine point one percent from a year before. The biggest yearly jump in more than forty years.
Now the really long view. Something that cost one dollar in nineteen thirteen cost about thirty-two dollars and fifty cents in twenty twenty-five.

That works out to a little over three percent a year, on average, for more than a century. Put the other way, a nineteen thirteen dollar now buys about three cents' worth. Ninety-seven percent of its buying power, gone. So why do prices keep rising at all?
Chapter three. What causes it.
Economists usually point to three engines. Demand. Supply shocks. And money and credit.
First, demand. When people, businesses and governments try to buy more than the economy can make, sellers raise prices. Too much money chasing too few goods.

Second, supply shocks. When something essential suddenly gets scarce or expensive, like oil, the cost ripples through everything. In June twenty twenty-two, energy prices were up forty-two percent in a year. Gasoline, sixty percent.

visual.title: 2 · Supply shock: June 2022 vs a year earlier

scenes.say: And it's happening again. In the year to September, energy rose about twenty percent and gasoline thirty-four. But prices without food and energy rose just two point six percent.

Third, money and credit. When borrowing is cheap and money flows freely, spending can outrun what the economy produces. The Federal Reserve itself says inflation over the longer run is primarily determined by monetary policy.

visual.source: Federal Reserve, Statement on Longer-Run Goals (reaffirmed Jan 2026)

scenes.say: And inflation can feed itself. If people expect higher prices, workers push for bigger raises, businesses raise prices to cover them, and the cycle keeps turning. So who's supposed to stop it?
Chapter four. Why the Fed aims for two percent.

The US Federal Reserve aims for inflation of two percent a year, measured by a cousin of the C-P-I called the P-C-E price index. It made that goal official in January twenty twelve, and reaffirmed it this January.

visual.label: the Fed's longer-run inflation goal
visual.sub: PCE price index · adopted 2012, reaffirmed Jan 2026

scenes.say: Why not zero? A St. Louis Fed economist gives three reasons. Price measures may run slightly high, so two percent measured may be closer to zero in reality. Falling prices, called deflation, may do more harm. And a little inflation leaves room to cut interest rates in a recession. Not every economist agrees.

visual.title: Why not 0%?
items: Price measures may run a little high
Room to cut rates in a recession

scenes.say: The Fed's main tool is interest rates. To fight the twenty twenty-two surge, it raised its key rate from near zero in March twenty twenty-two to five and a quarter to five and a half percent by July twenty twenty-three. It cut rates in twenty twenty-four and twenty twenty-five, to three and a half to three and three-quarters percent. Then this September, with inflation elevated again, it raised them a quarter point, to between three and three-quarters and four percent, where they stood as this video was made.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive. People and businesses spend less, and price pressure cools. But it works with a lag, so the Fed is always steering by the rear-view mirror.

And even the target adds up. At two percent, prices double about every thirty-five years. At three point seven percent, about every nineteen. But inflation doesn't hit everyone the same way. Some people actually win.

visual.title: Years for prices to double
visual.note: If inflation stayed at that rate · simple math, not a forecast

scenes.say: Chapter five. Who wins and who loses.

Start with the losers. Cash savers. Money in a drawer, or in an account paying less than inflation, loses buying power every year. The national average savings rate is just zero point three nine percent, according to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.

Now the winners. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans. Say your fixed mortgage payment, principal and interest, is two thousand dollars a month. If prices rise three percent a year, in ten years that payment feels like about fourteen hundred and ninety in today's money. In twenty years, about eleven hundred.

visual.title: A fixed $2,000 loan payment, in today's dollars (example)
visual.note: Example: principal & interest only, 3% inflation a year · only helps if your income keeps up

scenes.say: That's the twist. Inflation quietly moves value from lenders to fixed-rate borrowers. The bank gets paid back in cheaper dollars, especially when inflation turns out higher than expected when the loan was made, and as long as the borrower's income keeps rising.

Workers are in the middle. It depends on whether pay keeps up. In the year to June twenty twenty-two, average hourly pay rose about five percent, but prices rose about nine. So real pay, meaning pay after inflation, fell three point six percent. In the year to September twenty twenty-six, average pay rose three percent, but prices rose three point seven. Real pay fell zero point seven percent.

visual.title: US average hourly pay vs prices (seasonally adjusted)

scenes.say: So, roughly. Cash savers and lenders tend to lose. Fixed-rate borrowers tend to win. Workers win or lose depending on their raises. To know which side you're on, you need one simple formula.

visual.title: Who inflation hits
items: Cash savers & lenders: tend to lose

scenes.say: Chapter six. The math of buying power.
Here it is. Your real return is one plus your interest rate, divided by one plus inflation, minus one. As a shortcut: your rate minus inflation.

That's why our drawer lost about three hundred and sixty dollars, not three hundred and seventy. Prices rose three point seven four percent, and ten thousand divided by one point zero three seven four is about nine thousand six hundred and forty.

Now compare three homes for that ten thousand over the same year, before tax. In cash, down about three hundred and sixty. At the average savings rate, down about three hundred and twenty-three. At three and a half percent, an example rate, not a quote, down only about twenty-three.

visual.title: $10,000 for a year, before tax (Sept 2025 → Sept 2026)

scenes.say: Here's that last one, step by step. Ten thousand, plus three hundred and fifty of interest, minus about three hundred and seventy-three lost to higher prices. You end with about nine thousand nine hundred and seventy-seven in buying power.

Over twenty years, at three percent inflation, the gap gets huge. Cash ends up worth about five thousand five hundred in today's money. At three and a half percent, about eleven thousand, before tax. So what can you actually do?
Chapter seven. What you can do.
Here are four practical moves. None of them is a product pitch, and none of them is magic.

First, your emergency fund. It needs to be safe and easy to reach, so it shouldn't swing with markets. But it doesn't have to earn nothing. Some banks pay more than the national average, and rates change, so compare.

Second, inflation-protected bonds from the US Treasury. With TIPS, the principal rises with the C-P-I and interest is paid on the adjusted amount. Held to maturity, you never get back less than the original principal. I bonds work differently: the rate itself has an inflation part that resets every six months.

I bonds bought from November twenty twenty-six to April twenty twenty-seven start at five point five one percent, including a one point four percent fixed part that lasts for the life of the bond. But there are trade-offs. You can buy up to ten thousand dollars a year electronically. You can't cash out for twelve months. And before five years, you lose the last three months of interest.

visual.title: I bonds: the fine print (1.40% of the rate is fixed for life)

scenes.say: These are built to keep pace with inflation, not to make you rich. Whether they fit depends on your goals and your timeline.

visual.text:
Built to keep pace,
not to get rich.

scenes.say: Third, money you won't need for many years. Over long periods, a diversified mix of investments has historically had a better chance of beating inflation than cash. But it can fall sharply, sometimes for years, and past results don't guarantee future ones.

visual.title: Match the money to the timeline

right.label: Needed in 10+ yrs
right.sub: can beat prices, can also fall

visual.verdict: Not advice · investments can lose value

scenes.say: Fourth, check your raise against inflation. A three percent raise in a year when prices rise three point seven percent is a small pay cut in disguise.

visual.label: a 3.0% raise when prices rise 3.7%
visual.sub: your real raise · use the formula

scenes.say: Inflation never takes your money. It takes what your money can do. Now you know how to measure it, and how to keep up.

visual.title: Measure it. Keep up.
visual.sub: inflation takes what your money can do
